title: Animal Migration: Where's that gnu gnoing?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss animal migration: examples such as wildebeest, monarch butterflies, fruit bats in Zambia, elk, caribou, and dogs going to their food bowl. They cover why animals migrate (food, water, breeding/mating, climate, survival), and the types of migration (irruptive, eruptive, complete and partial, altitudinal, and removal migration). They also discuss whales feeding at the poles and calving near the equator, chinook salmon returning to their natal spawning site, and the whooping crane, whose eastern population was wiped out and which was taught its migration route by an ultralight aircraft flight from Wisconsin to Florida. The episode ends mid-discussion of photoperiod and circadian rhythm as migration cues.

segments.title: Opening banter and animal migration examples
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the show and ask whether the other has seen animals migrate. They mention dogs going to the food bowl, monarch butterflies, fruit bats in Zambia, elk and caribou.

segments.title: Wildebeest river drowning
segments.summary: The hosts discuss wildebeest (gnus) migration and a 2007 event in Kenya where around ten thousand animals crossed a river, and some drowned after one went in and was swept away.

segments.title: Defining migration and reasons for it
segments.summary: Josh defines migration as a large-scale movement of an animal species, usually driven by food, water, mating, or climate. Chuck notes that the dogs' trips to the food bowl count as migration.

segments.title: Types of migration
segments.summary: The hosts list migration types: irruptive (unpredictable) and eruptive migration (wildebeest follow water and thunderclouds), complete and partial migration (barn owl), altitudinal migration (goats moving down mountains), and removal migration, where a species leaves a habitat permanently.

segments.title: Whales and chinook salmon
segments.summary: Whales migrate to the poles to feed on krill and to the equator to breed and calve. Chinook salmon return to the river where they were born to spawn.

segments.title: Whooping crane removal and ultralight migration
segments.summary: The eastern whooping crane population was wiped out, and the western population kept the species alive. Rutgers ornithologists bred them in captivity. Because the migration route was lost, a man in an ultralight aircraft dressed as a whooping crane led birds from Wisconsin to Florida after they were raised with the aircraft's sound.

segments.title: Migration cues: photoperiod and circadian rhythm
segments.summary: Hosts note that how animals know when to migrate is still partly a mystery, and begin to introduce photoperiod and circadian rhythm as possible cues. The transcript ends mid-sentence.
